hero.title: See what is on, without seeing what is private
hero.lead: calbridge mirrors calendars across Google, Microsoft 365 and iCloud, at exactly the amount of detail each recipient should see.

problem.title: One person, several calendars, no shared view
problem.body: Work, private life and the people you share a calendar with each live in their own account. No provider shows all of them in one place, and none lets a work calendar see only that a slot is busy while a private calendar keeps the full details. Typing placeholder events by hand drifts out of date within a day and hides real conflicts.

detailLevels.title: One connection, three levels of detail
detailLevels.lead: A connection between two calendars copies events in one direction, at a detail level chosen for that connection alone.

full.title: Full
full.body: Title, time, description, location and attendees copy across unchanged.

titleTime.title: Title and time
titleTime.body: Only the title and the time copy across. Nobody downstream sees the description, the location or who else is invited.

busyBlock.title: Busy or free only
busyBlock.body: Only whether the time is busy or free copies across: no title, no description, nothing else. A work calendar can show a slot is taken without ever learning why.

cta.title: Ready to connect your calendars?
cta.body: Sign in or create an account in the application to start connecting calendars.

pricing.title: Pricing
pricing.body: There are no prices yet, because there is nothing to buy yet: the service runs for its operator's own use. This page carries real pricing once that changes.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.lead: What calbridge stores, why, and what this application never sees.

intro.heading: About this text
intro.body: This text describes what calbridge's own source code actually stores, encrypts, shares and deletes. It is not a legal review and not a data processing agreement; whoever operates this deployment is responsible for running it and for this text.

notInOperation.heading: What is not in operation yet
notInOperation.body: calbridge is built in steps, and this text describes the software as it runs today rather than as it is designed. Three parts of that design are not wired into the running service yet: there is no way to connect a calendar account, so no calendar credentials are stored; no event is therefore copied into any calendar; and the part that tears a connection down and takes back the events it wrote exists and is tested, but nothing in the running service calls it. Each section below says which of that applies today.

account.heading: A local account with a password
account.body: A local account stores its email address, a password hash computed with Argon2id, and, once set up, the two-factor (TOTP) secret and the counter of the last accepted code. Alongside those are the account's status (active or disabled) and the timestamps of when it was created and last changed. The password itself is never stored, only its hash. These fields live in the users table.

providerSignIn.heading: Signing in with Google, Microsoft or Apple
providerSignIn.body: Signing in with a provider asks for identity only, never for calendar access: Google and Microsoft are asked for the openid, profile and email scopes, Apple for openid alone. The identities table holds the provider's own fixed identifier for the account (its "subject"), the provider's name, and when the row was created. Google supplies a verified email address, which the account then uses. Microsoft never marks an email address as verified, and calbridge never asks Apple for one at all; in both cases the account gets a placeholder address instead, under the unreachable domain sign-in.calbridge.invalid, derived from a hash of the provider and the subject, never from the real address.
providerSignIn.linkBody: A provider sign-in is never linked to a calendar connection someone else made with the same provider account: that separation is structural in the code, not only a rule, because the part of the application handling sign-in has no access to the calendar connections table at all.

calendarConnections.heading: Connected calendar accounts
calendarConnections.body: Connecting a calendar account is a second, separate step after signing in. CalDAV is the only connector calbridge has, with iCloud as its first server profile, so a CalDAV account is what could be connected today: for iCloud an Apple ID with an app-specific password, because Apple offers no OAuth flow for calendars. The running service has no endpoint for creating such a connection yet, so no calendar credentials are stored here at the moment.
calendarConnections.encryptionBody: Where one is stored, it is stored encrypted: the storage layer encrypts it with AES-256-GCM before it reaches the database and decrypts it again on the way back out, so the database itself never holds the plain form. The key lives with the owner of this deployment and is supplied through the ENCRYPTION_KEY environment variable. That is encryption at rest, not end-to-end encryption: a connector needs the password to reach the server, so the decrypted credential sits in the application's memory while it is in use. It is never written anywhere unencrypted, and it does not appear in log lines or error messages: the code holding it replaces it with a placeholder there.

syncData.heading: What a connection between two calendars stores
syncData.body: For every event a connection (edge) copies, calbridge keeps one small row in a mapping table (event_mapping): the connection's id, the event's id in the source, the id of its copy in the target, the event's start and end, a content hash, plus the owning account and the timestamps of when the row was created and last changed. The same row holds an encrypted cache of the copied title and description; it is filled only when the chosen detail level copies such content at all.
syncData.busyBlockBody: At the "busy or free only" detail level, calbridge copies nothing but whether a time range is busy and whether the event is happening: for such a connection, no title, description, location, attendee or recurrence rule is written into the target calendar or stored, and the mapping row's encrypted cache stays empty. What the sync receives from a connector is the complete event: it is read in memory to decide what to copy and to compute the content hash that tells a change from an unchanged run. The detail level governs what is written and what is stored, not what the sync is handed.

handEdits.heading: A copy edited by hand
handEdits.body: Editing a copy calbridge wrote into a target calendar by hand does not keep that edit: the next sync overwrites it without comment, because a copy is a projection of its source, and only the source counts as the truth. A note added to a mirrored copy does not survive.
handEdits.exceptionBody: One edit does survive, for a technical reason rather than as a promise: a single changed occurrence of a repeating event, in a calendar that keeps such changes inside the repeating event's own object. No identifier addresses that occurrence on its own there, so the sync pass leaves it alone.

sharing.heading: Sharing a calendar with someone else
sharing.body: Sharing one of your own calendars with someone else sets the maximum detail level that share allows. Revoking such a share removes the share itself, at once.
sharing.teardownBody: Tearing down the connections built on it, and taking back the events they wrote, is a separate step the running service does not perform yet. The part that tears a connection down — first every event it wrote into the target calendar, then the matching rows of the mapping table, the target calendar calbridge created for it where it created one, and finally the connection itself — exists and is tested, but nothing in the running service calls it. Until that is wired, the connections stay in place after a share is revoked. Nothing has been written anywhere so far, because no calendar account can be connected yet. Once the step is wired, sharing again will not bring the connection back; it has to be rebuilt.

deletion.heading: Deleting your account
deletion.body: Deleting your own account removes, in one transaction: every row in the mapping table, every connection, every share you gave and every one you received, every calendar, every connected calendar account together with its encrypted credentials, every sign-in identity, and finally the account itself. Every signed-in session for that account ends at the same time.
deletion.limitBody: One limit remains: an event a connection already wrote into a calendar at the provider is not removed there when the account is deleted, because that would need reaching that provider, which deleting an account does not do. Deleting a single connection is meant to take its copies with it, and the part that does so exists and is tested; the running service does not call that one either yet. So today neither path removes anything from a calendar at the provider. Nothing has been written into one so far, because no calendar account can be connected yet.

noAnalytics.heading: No analytics, no third parties
noAnalytics.body: Neither this site nor the application loads an analytics or tracking service, a third-party embed, or a font fetched from another server at runtime. There is nothing of that kind to disclose, because none of it is included.

session.heading: Session cookie
session.body: Once signed in, the application sets a session cookie whose only purpose is to recognise that signed-in session. It is never used for any other account or any other site, and it ends at the latest when you log out or delete your account.
